title: Hegelian Philosophy: Consciousness and the Problem of Knowing
question: Hegel begins by rejecting the picture of cognition as a detachable instrument for reaching a reality already fixed outside it. Experience tests consciousness by its own shifting standards, not by a criterion imported from nowhere.
tags: Consciousness and the Problem of Knowing
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Sense-Certainty and Perception
question: A demonstrative such as 'this' seems maximally concrete, yet is repeatable across countless objects and moments. Hegel turns this difficulty into an inquiry about the mediating role of universality.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Force, Understanding, and Infinity
question: The understanding posits hidden laws behind appearances, yet its explanatory divisions repeatedly reproduce the movement they were meant to arrest.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Self-Consciousness and Recognition
question: Self-consciousness cannot secure independence merely by consuming objects; recognition requires encountering another self-consciousness. The famous struggle is therefore relational, not a simple celebration of domination.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Stoicism, Skepticism, Unhappy Consciousness
question: Each posture seeks freedom but encounters a different difficulty in locating its truth: in thought alone, in negation, or in a divided relation to an immutable beyond.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Reason and Ethical Life
question: Reason first seeks itself in nature and action; it later confronts objective patterns of ethical life that cannot be reduced to an isolated mind.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Spirit, Culture, and Alienation
question: Spirit is not a ghostly thing above society, but a pattern of historically mediated communal self-understanding. Its moments include estrangement, conflict, and attempts at reconciliation.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Religion and Absolute Knowing
question: The end of the Phenomenology concerns how a truth first presented in images or representation can be comprehended conceptually. Absolute knowing is not knowing every empirical fact.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Logic: Being, Essence, Concept
question: The Science of Logic attempts to develop categories through their own inadequacies, moving beyond external taxonomies and fixed definitions.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Hegelian Philosophy: Hegel's Legacy and Criticism
question: Hegel's work has inspired metaphysics, social theory, and theories of recognition. Critiques question closure, teleology, freedom, Eurocentrism, and the status of dialectical necessity.
sources: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Science of Logic (1812–1816)

title: Post-Structuralism: Structures and Their Limits
question: Structuralist models explain meanings through relational differences. Post-structuralist approaches explore the instability, history, power, and material practices that complicate a closed structure.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Foucault: Knowledge and Power
question: For Foucault, knowledge is entangled with historically variable procedures that constitute objects of inquiry. This is not the claim that every assertion is false or merely propaganda.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Discipline and Biopolitics
question: Modern power also operates through routines, norms, and the management of populations, not solely by spectacular prohibitions.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Deleuze: Difference and Repetition
question: Deleuze criticizes the subordination of difference to identity and seeks productive multiplicities. Repetition is not reducible to copying the same thing.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Deleuze and Guattari
question: Desire is not merely lack in their account: it participates in social and material production. Their concepts are not literal maps of biology.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Barthes: Author, Reader, Text
question: Barthes challenges interpretive sovereignty assigned to an author's intention and attends to how cultural codes circulate in reading.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Kristeva and the Semiotic
question: Language and subjectivity are treated as crossed by social signification and embodied drives; boundaries of the self are not simply given.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Difference, Identity, and Politics
question: Post-structuralist approaches have been productive in critiques of gender and identity, while remaining contested about agency and normative grounds.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Reading Methods and Objections
question: A good reading neither dismisses these traditions as relativism nor immunizes them against criticism. Reconstruct their claims carefully and ask what could count against them.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Post-Structuralism: Post-Structuralist Legacies
question: The traditions differ substantially: Foucault's genealogy is not Deleuze's ontology, and Derrida's deconstruction is not a universal method of disbelief.
sources: Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Gilles Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (1968)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: The Modern and the Postmodern
question: 'Postmodern' names disputed conditions and styles, not one doctrine. Begin by separating accounts of social change from philosophical claims about reason and truth.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Lyotard and Legitimation
question: Lyotard examines how knowledge is authorized when universal emancipatory stories lose credibility. This diagnosis must not be simplified into 'all claims are equally true.'
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Baudrillard and Simulation
question: Baudrillard argues that in contemporary mediated culture signs can organize experience without simply representing a prior stable reality.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Jameson and Late Capitalism
question: Jameson relates postmodern cultural forms to transformations in capitalist production. His approach differs from treating postmodernism as merely an artistic choice.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Rorty and Ironism
question: Rorty challenges the demand that inquiry mirror nature from an ahistorical standpoint, yet continues to defend practical conversation and liberal solidarity.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: The Subject and the Fragment
question: Some postmodern thought questions the coherent autonomous self presumed in classical modernity, while critics ask whether agency survives such critique.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Art, Architecture, and Irony
question: Postmodern cultural forms often incorporate quotation, stylistic mixture, and self-conscious artifice rather than the unity demanded by some modernist programs.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Critiques: Habermas and Others
question: Habermas disputes accounts that abandon modernity's unfinished emancipatory promise; others question sweeping accounts of fragmentation.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Science, Truth, and Relativism
question: Distinguish fallibilism from relativism. Questioning grand narratives does not automatically refute experimental evidence or make contradictory claims equally justified.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Postmodern Philosophy: Postmodern Debates Today
question: Test broad claims against concrete cases and avoid treating 'postmodern' as a synonym for nihilism or obscurity.
sources: Jean-François Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979); Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Metaphysics of Presence
question: Derrida studies philosophical traditions privileging presence, self-identity, and immediate meaning. Deconstruction reads how such positions depend on what they subordinate.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Saussure and the Sign
question: Derrida inherits differential accounts of language yet questions the idea of a final signified that arrests signification.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Différance
question: The coined term gathers differing and deferring without referring to a new substantial thing. It problematizes the aspiration to a simply present origin of meaning.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Deconstruction in Practice
question: Deconstruction is not arbitrary reversal or destruction. It investigates internal tensions by patiently reconstructing a text's arguments and exclusions.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Of Grammatology
question: Derrida reads Rousseau and broader philosophical assumptions about writing as a mere supplement to living speech. The supplement also reveals a lack in the allegedly complete original.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Speech and Phenomena
question: Derrida engages Husserl's distinction between expression and indication and asks whether temporal retention disrupts perfect self-presence.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Signature, Event, Context
question: If a mark can function only through repeatability, its contexts cannot be absolutely saturated. This does not imply every interpretation is equally plausible.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)

title: Deconstruction & Derrida: Justice, Law, and Hospitality
question: Derrida distinguishes calculable law from an incalculable demand of justice, investigating the necessity and difficulty of decisions under conditions of uncertainty.
sources: Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967); Limited Inc (1988)
